title: Planning a Hub installation
description: Understand the deployment building blocks and the configuration work that follows installation.

chapters.title: A deployment, not just a web page

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional company bringing Hub into its own infrastructure. The interface looks like a website, so can the administrator install a single web container and call it a day?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The interface is only part of the system. The installation guide describes several services deployed into Kubernetes. Helm helps package their configuration and resources so the administrator can manage a coordinated deployment instead of a pile of unrelated containers.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: A box of building blocks, with an assembly plan?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: That's a useful picture. The important part is understanding which services depend on each other and who will operate them. The guide links to the deployment repository for the actual installation instructions rather than trying to make this overview a universal recipe.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should our administrator look at before pressing ahead?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Review the supporting services listed in the guide, including the database, messaging and connectivity components. Their availability matters to the application. Plan the environment and read the current deployment instructions before choosing installation values.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So a running frontend isn't proof the whole system is ready?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Right. A page can load while another part of the chain is misconfigured. Verify an end-to-end activity that matters to your users, not only that a container started. Keep the current deployment repository as the source for exact dependencies and settings.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's say the deployment is running. What does the company do next?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Move into application configuration. Installing services provides the environment; configuring Hub connects that environment to the team's resources and intended use. The configuration guide is the next stop rather than guessing settings from a screenshot.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That's the difference between opening a new office and deciding who works in each room.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Treat the initial installation as a beginning. Check the relevant integrations, access and operational behaviour before handing the system over to the whole team. A small, verified setup is easier to reason about than many changes at once.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: One practical example: the site address field doesn't suggest any places. Is that necessarily a broken installation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Not necessarily. Address suggestions need the documented Google Maps and Places setup, including the newer Places API, billing and the correct browser key restrictions. A key enabled only for the legacy API isn't enough.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And making the key visible to the browser doesn't mean leaving it unrestricted?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. Restrict it to the intended websites and APIs, including the actual origin used for development. Follow the guide's verification steps and inspect explicit browser errors. Keep credentials and configuration out of this audio; the linked instructions have the precise fields.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
